why: The starter builds the id from the user name, so anyone who has seen `token-ada` can type `token-bo`. A session id is a bearer credential: whoever presents it is that user. It has to come from a random source, and `randHex(16)` gives 128 bits nobody can derive or guess.

The starter's row records only who the session belongs to. Without `created` and `lastSeen` the server can't tell how old a session is or when it was last used, so the timeouts later in this unit would have nothing to measure.

The starter writes only `Path`, `Max-Age` and `HttpOnly`, so the cookie never gets `Secure` or `SameSite`. It also tests `opts.maxAge` for truthiness, which silently drops `maxAge: 0`. Collecting the parts in an array and checking `!= null` writes every attribute that was set, including a zero.

The starter puts any name and value straight into the header. A value like `abc; Domain=evil.example` then adds an attribute the server never chose. Checking both against the cookie grammar, and throwing a `TypeError` when they don't match, keeps the header exactly what the caller asked for.

`part.split("=")` splits on every `=`, and destructuring keeps only the first two pieces, so `next=/a?b=c` loses its `=c`. Cutting at the first `=` with `indexOf` keeps the rest of the value intact. Skipping pieces with no `=` and names already seen stops odd headers from overwriting a real cookie.

The starter finds the session the visitor arrived with and marks it as logged in. If an attacker planted that id, the attacker's copy now opens the victim's account. Deleting the old row and creating a fresh one at login leaves the planted id pointing at nothing.

The starter's login answers with a brand-new session and an empty cart, so anything the visitor added before signing in is lost. Carrying `cart` from the old row into the new one, and sending that new id in `Set-Cookie`, makes the rotation invisible to the shopper.

The starter's `touchSession` returns any row it finds, however old, and never updates it. A session nobody checks against the clock never ends, and one whose `lastSeen` never moves can't have an idle timeout. Read `now()` once, end the session when either limit is reached, and only then slide `lastSeen` forward.

The starter's clearing cookie is `sid=; Max-Age=0` with no `Path`. Browsers match a cookie by name and path, so that header can leave the original `sid` in place. Building it with `serializeCookie` and the same `Path=/` the session cookie was set with actually replaces it.

The starter only tells the browser to forget the cookie; the row stays on the server. Anyone holding a copy of the id (a proxy log, malware, the fixation attacker) keeps using it until it times out. Deleting the row is what makes logout real.

The starter has no `/api/logout-all` route, so it answers 404. Signing out everywhere means finding every row with the caller's `userName` and deleting them all, which is only possible because a session is a row the server can search.

The starter's encoder never reads the bytes, so it returns an empty string. base64url takes the bytes three at a time as one 24-bit number and writes four 6-bit characters, or two or three for a short final group, with no `=` padding.

The starter's decoder returns an empty array for every input. Decoding runs the encoder backwards: each character is worth 6 bits, and a byte comes out whenever 8 bits have built up. It also has to throw for a character outside the alphabet and for a length that leaves one stray character.

The starter's `sign` returns only the encoded payload, with no signature, so anyone could write their own token. Appending a dot and the base64url HMAC of the payload means only a holder of `SECRET` can produce a token that matches.

The starter's `verify` decodes whatever payload it gets and never checks a signature, so an edited `role: "admin"` goes straight through. Recompute the HMAC and refuse a mismatch first; only then parse the payload, inside a `try`, so a malformed token is `null` rather than an exception.

The starter's loop returns at the first byte that differs, so a signature wrong in byte 0 is rejected sooner than one wrong in byte 31. Measured over many requests, that difference gives a valid signature away byte by byte. OR-ing every byte's XOR into one number and checking it once at the end costs the same whatever the input.

The starter's `verify` still compares base64url strings with `!==`, which stops at the first different character and never calls `safeEqual`. Decoding the given signature to bytes (refusing one that won't decode) and comparing with `safeEqual` closes the leak where it matters.

The starter ignores the `kid` and tries every key until one matches, so the label means nothing: a token that says `2026-09` but was signed with August's key still passes, and an unknown `kid` costs one HMAC per key. Looking the `kid` up with `hasOwnProperty` and checking only that key fixes both.

The starter's `rotateKey` does nothing, so `sign` keeps using the old key. Rotating adds the new secret and switches `currentKid` to it, and it refuses a `kid` that already exists, because silently replacing a secret breaks every token it signed.

The starter's `retireKey` does nothing, so a retired key keeps verifying its tokens forever. Deleting it from `KEYS` ends them, and refusing to delete `currentKid` stops every newly signed token from failing at once.

The starter's `decodeJwt` returns `null` for every token, so it never shows what a JWT carries. A JWT is three base64url parts: the first two are JSON anyone can read with `readPart`, and the third is the signature, kept as text. Reading them inside a `try` makes a malformed token `null` instead of an exception.

The starter copies the whole user record into the token, so the email, password hash and reset token travel with every request, readable by anyone who decodes it. Building the claims by hand keeps the token to what the server needs next time: who (`sub`), what they may do (`role`) and when (`iat`, `exp`).

The starter's `forgeNone` returns an empty string, which isn't a JWT at all. An unsecured JWT is still three parts: a header saying `alg: "none"`, the claims, and an empty signature after the last dot.

The starter keeps the legacy rule that returns the payload whenever the header says `none`, so the token decides how it gets checked. Allowing exactly `HS256`, and refusing a header that isn't an object, puts that decision back on the server: `none` in any spelling, `HS512` and a missing `alg` all fall out.

The starter's `acceptToken` returns any correctly signed token, so an expired one, one not valid yet, one from another issuer and one meant for another API all get in. Each claim needs its own check, in seconds (`Math.floor(now() / 1000)`) with `LEEWAY` for clock drift. All four checks live in this one block, which is why the later checkpoints pass once this one does.

The starter stores the raw refresh token as the Map key and records no family or `used` flag. A leaked table would hand out working tokens, and there would be nothing to rotate or revoke. Keying by `sha256(refresh)` and recording the family with `used: false` gives each refresh token a row the server can reason about.

The starter hands back the same refresh token every time and never notices one being used twice. Rotation marks the old row `used` and issues a new token in the same family, and a used token that comes back means someone copied it, so every token in that family is deleted. The lookup also has to go by `sha256`, since that is how the rows are stored.
The starter returns the claims for any token whose header says `alg: none`, so an unsigned token claiming to be admin gets in. The server allows exactly `HS256` and refuses everything else.

The starter checks `exp` and `iss` but never `aud`, so a token the same auth server issued for `billing-api` opens `notes-api` too. Normalise `aud` to an array and refuse a token that doesn't name this API.

The starter's `LEEWAY` is 60000, a millisecond-sized number used in a check where every time is in seconds. That is almost 17 hours of drift allowance, so a token that expired two hours ago still passes. JWT times are seconds, so the leeway is 60.

The starter compares base64url strings with `!==`, which stops at the first different character, so rejecting a bad signature takes longer the more of it is right. Decode the signature to bytes (a bad encoding is `null`) and compare with `safeEqual`, which reads every byte whatever it finds.

The starter falls back to the first key in `KEYS` when it doesn't recognise the token's `kid`, so a token naming a key that doesn't exist is still checked, and accepted, against some other key. Refuse a `kid` that isn't one of `KEYS`' own properties before any HMAC runs.
